In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20, as shown in FIG. 2.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24 shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

All five sheets' failures were drawing defects, so I repaired them in the figure briefs and kept the text in sync without touching the claims, numeral table, or disclosed subject matter.

**FIG. 1** (leaders for 10, 24, 36 converging; 10 landing on the tile's front edge): the composition now places the machine on the left of the tile with a wide open expanse of tile to the right, so the three targets sit in three separated regions. Numeral 10 targets the outer silhouette running down the left side of the machine above the base, explicitly clear of the covering element; 24 targets the long front stretch of the band, which is now specified deep enough for its front surface to read plainly; 36 targets the open tile expanse to the right, away from the machine and the tile outlines.

**FIG. 2** (missing connection line; base rendered as two blocks with a gap): the connection line was an invented rendering constraint, and it was what produced the gap through the slab. The brief now shows fluid communication schematically by the housing standing on the slab above the chamber, and states positively that the slab is a single unbroken hatched body with no gap, slot, opening, duct, port, or vertical line dividing it. The Brief Description of the Drawings and the corresponding detailed-description sentence were reworded to match what the sheet shows, with the fluid communication itself still stated as the disclosure requires.

**FIG. 3** (three nested rectangles): the sheet is now specified as one rectangular ring, a band with a rectangular opening drawn with exactly two closed lines, with the slab's outer edge expressly falling on the ring's outer edge and no third rectangle, frame, or border anywhere.

**FIG. 4** (38 converging with 26): the column is now drawn narrower than the bands and over the left-hand part of the area, so a wide open stretch of the covering element's top edge line lies to the right of it. Numeral 38 targets that open stretch, well away from the column; 26 stays on the line closing the column's bottom, within the column's width; the clearance is required to stand plainly open.

**FIG. 5** (no terminal dot on 46; 24 landing on a corner): the pulling element is now one unbroken curved path of even thickness crossing an open expanse of tile and broken off well inside the drawing area, targeted on that stretch clear of the machine; 24 targets the long front stretch of the band, away from either end where it turns, with the band again deep enough to read as a visible surface.

I also removed over-specification while making these changes (redundant view boilerplate, the "so that the clearance is unmistakable" flourish, restated geometry in the clearance bullet), so every brief stays within the length limit. Numeral assignments per sheet are unchanged: 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44 / 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36 / 16, 24 / 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 / 10, 24, 36, 46, covering all sixteen numerals with at most seven on a sheet.

input.summary: Repaired all five failing drawing sheets by rewriting the figure briefs, and synchronized the two sentences of application text that described what FIG. 2 shows. No claim, numeral definition, or disclosed embodiment was changed. FIG. 1 now separates the converging targets for 10, 24 and 36 into three distinct regions and steers 10 onto the machine silhouette well away from the tile. FIG. 2 drops the connection line that the renderer kept turning into a gap through the base, shows fluid communication by the housing standing on the slab above the chamber, and states affirmatively that the slab is one unbroken hatched body. FIG. 3 is respecified as a single rectangular ring drawn with exactly two closed lines, with the slab edge falling on the ring's outer edge and no third rectangle permitted. FIG. 4 narrows the column and moves the exposed face 38 anchor onto the open stretch of the covering element's top edge line to the right of the column, separating it from bearing face 26. FIG. 5 gives the pulling element 46 a single unbroken curved path across open tile with a broad target on it, and moves 24 onto the long front stretch of the band, away from the corners.
reasoning: FIG. 1's three convergence failures shared one cause: the machine sat centered on the tile with a shallow band, so the silhouette, the band's front surface and the tile surface all met in the same lower region. Rather than fiddling with endpoint wording, I changed the composition: machine on the left of the tile, a wide open tile expanse on the right, and a band deep enough for its front surface to read as a surface. Numeral 10 now targets the silhouette running down the left side above the base, expressly clear of the covering element, which is exactly where the rejected dot went wrong; 36 targets the open expanse on the right; 24 targets the long front stretch of the band. Three targets, three separated regions.

FIG. 2's failure was caused by the brief itself. Asking for a plain line from the housing down across the hatched slab to the chamber invited the image model to open a duct, and it drew a full-height gap that split the base into two blocks. The line was never required by the disclosure, only by the brief, so I removed it and had the sheet indicate fluid communication by adjacency instead, with an explicit prohibition on any gap, slot, opening, duct, port or vertical line through the slab. Because the sheet no longer purports to draw the communication path, I reworded the FIG. 2 entry in the Brief Description and the one detailed-description sentence that pointed at FIG. 2, so the text describes what is actually depicted while still stating the fluid communication itself, which is disclosure-grounded.

FIG. 3 kept gaining a third rectangle because the brief described the loop as two nested rectangles, which reads as an instruction to draw rectangles and leaves the model free to add the slab outline as another one. I reframed it as a single object, a rectangular ring, that necessarily has two closed outlines, said in terms that the slab's outer edge falls on the ring's outer edge so no separate outline exists for it, and barred any further rectangle, frame or border. Same geometry, but described as one body rather than as a count of shapes.

FIG. 4's ungrounded 38 anchor was a geometry problem, not a wording problem: the bearing face line and the exposed face line are separated only by the clearance, so any two anchors on them converge. I separated them along the sheet instead of across it, by making the column narrower than the bands and standing over the left-hand part of the area, leaving an open stretch of the exposed face line to the right for 38 while 26 stays on the bottom line of the column. This is a fragmentary enlarged view, so a column narrower than the bands is an ordinary depiction, not an added structural feature.

FIG. 5's missing terminal dot on 46 and the corner hit on 24 both came from thin, ambiguous target geometry. The pulling element is now one unbroken curved path of even thickness crossing an open expanse of tile and broken off well inside the drawing area, with a broad target anywhere on that stretch; the band gets the same visible-front-surface treatment as FIG. 1 and its target is the long stretch facing the viewer, away from either end where the band turns, which is the language the rejecting reviews were applying.

I resisted the temptation to fix any of these by changing the patent text. The connection line, the column proportions and the ring framing are all depiction conventions confined to the briefs; nothing about a duct, a port, a ledge, or a handle shape entered the description, the claims or the numeral table. The only text edits were the two sentences describing what FIG. 2 shows, and they were narrowed to the depiction rather than widened.

Trimming was necessary because the repairs added constraint sentences and every brief was already close to the length ceiling. I cut redundant view boilerplate and restated geometry rather than any of the new endpoint or topology constraints, so all five briefs now sit under the limit with the substantive instructions intact.

figures/FIG-2-...-THE-CHAMBER.md: removed the housing-to-chamber connection line; fluid communication now indicated only by the housing standing on the slab above the chamber, with no connection line, opening, duct, port or route drawn; added an affirmative requirement that the slab is a single unbroken hatched body with no gap, slot or vertical line dividing it; unchanged numeral set and endpoint targets otherwise.

figures/FIG-3-...-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md: respecified as one rectangular ring drawn with exactly two closed thin lines; the slab's outer edge is stated to fall on the ring's outer edge; any third rectangle, frame or border is barred; targets for 24 (band, straight stretch away from the corners) and 16 (plain field inside the inner edge) restated in ring terms.

figures/FIG-4-...-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md: column now stands over the left-hand part of the drawing area and is narrower than the bands, leaving an open stretch of the uppermost band's top edge line to the right; endpoint for 38 moved onto that open stretch, well away from the column; endpoint for 26 confined to the bottom line within the width of the column; clearance bullet shortened.

figures/FIG-5-...-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md: machine placed on the right of the tile with an open expanse to the left; pulling element 46 drawn as a single unbroken curved path of even thickness across the open tile, broken off well inside the drawing area, with a broad target on that stretch; band given a plainly visible front surface and endpoint for 24 set on its long stretch away from the turns; endpoint for 36 moved below the pulling element and away from the tile outlines.

draft/07-drawings.md: FIG. 2 entry reworded to say the air-extraction mechanism is shown schematically on the base above the chamber with which it is in fluid communication, matching the repaired sheet.

draft/08-detailed-description.md: the sentence on fluid communication now states the relationship and then says FIG. 2 shows the air-extraction mechanism 20 carried on the base 12 with the chamber 22 beneath the base 12, so the figure reference describes only what the sheet depicts.
input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; no claim, description, or background text bearing on the art was touched. Claim 1 continues to rest on the combination of a rigid low-friction perimeter member ending in a bearing face that deliberately leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an extraction rate that holds the chamber below atmospheric pressure under that continuous ingress, an all-rigid vibration transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. That combination departs from DE-202021002652-U1, whose rubber-elastic apron suction cups are the compliant member this invention excludes from the load path; from US-11408462-B2, whose peripheral wall is formed by elastic partitions contacting the surface and whose added frame member exists to stop that partition deforming; from US-10001245-B2, which gives up vacuum coupling and switches its generator to blower mode to move on an air cushion, whereas here holding and sliding are simultaneous; from US-11247858-B2, a vacuum lifter built around a perforated suction plate for lifting sheet material rather than transmitting vibration into a bedded workpiece; and from US-4934475-A, where vibration is used to reduce the holding force and propel the body along a wall, the opposite of delivering vibration into the workpiece while the differential holds the device down.

FIG. 2's missing line and split base are cured by deleting the connection-line requirement that produced the gap: fluid communication is now indicated by the housing standing on the slab above the chamber, and the brief states affirmatively that the slab is a single unbroken hatched body with nothing passing through it. FIG. 3 is respecified as one rectangular ring drawn with exactly two closed lines, with the slab edge falling on the ring's outer edge and no third rectangle, frame or border allowed. FIG. 4 separates the exposed face 38 anchor from the bearing face 26 anchor by making the column narrower than the bands and placing it over the left-hand part of the area, so 38 sits on the open stretch of the covering element's top edge line to the right of the column while 26 stays on the line closing the column's bottom. FIG. 5 gives the pulling element 46 one unbroken curved path of even thickness across open tile, broken off well inside the drawing area with a broad target on that stretch, and moves 24 onto the long front stretch of the band away from the corners. Nothing was added to the claims, description, numeral table or embodiments to accommodate the renderer; the numeral table is untouched, the same numerals remain on the same sheets, all sixteen numerals are still covered, no sheet carries more than seven, and every brief is within the length limit with no note, placeholder or human-directed instruction.

structured_output.summary: Repaired all five failing drawing sheets by rewriting the figure briefs, and synchronized the two sentences of application text that described what FIG. 2 shows. No claim, numeral definition, or disclosed embodiment was changed. FIG. 1 now separates the converging targets for 10, 24 and 36 into three distinct regions and steers 10 onto the machine silhouette well away from the tile. FIG. 2 drops the connection line that the renderer kept turning into a gap through the base, shows fluid communication by the housing standing on the slab above the chamber, and states affirmatively that the slab is one unbroken hatched body. FIG. 3 is respecified as a single rectangular ring drawn with exactly two closed lines, with the slab edge falling on the ring's outer edge and no third rectangle permitted. FIG. 4 narrows the column and moves the exposed face 38 anchor onto the open stretch of the covering element's top edge line to the right of the column, separating it from bearing face 26. FIG. 5 gives the pulling element 46 a single unbroken curved path across open tile with a broad target on it, and moves 24 onto the long front stretch of the band, away from the corners.
reasoning: FIG. 1's three convergence failures shared one cause: the machine sat centered on the tile with a shallow band, so the silhouette, the band's front surface and the tile surface all met in the same lower region. Rather than fiddling with endpoint wording, I changed the composition: machine on the left of the tile, a wide open tile expanse on the right, and a band deep enough for its front surface to read as a surface. Numeral 10 now targets the silhouette running down the left side above the base, expressly clear of the covering element, which is exactly where the rejected dot went wrong; 36 targets the open expanse on the right; 24 targets the long front stretch of the band. Three targets, three separated regions.

FIG. 2's failure was caused by the brief itself. Asking for a plain line from the housing down across the hatched slab to the chamber invited the image model to open a duct, and it drew a full-height gap that split the base into two blocks. The line was never required by the disclosure, only by the brief, so I removed it and had the sheet indicate fluid communication by adjacency instead, with an explicit prohibition on any gap, slot, opening, duct, port or vertical line through the slab. Because the sheet no longer purports to draw the communication path, I reworded the FIG. 2 entry in the Brief Description and the one detailed-description sentence that pointed at FIG. 2, so the text describes what is actually depicted while still stating the fluid communication itself, which is disclosure-grounded.

FIG. 3 kept gaining a third rectangle because the brief described the loop as two nested rectangles, which reads as an instruction to draw rectangles and leaves the model free to add the slab outline as another one. I reframed it as a single object, a rectangular ring, that necessarily has two closed outlines, said in terms that the slab's outer edge falls on the ring's outer edge so no separate outline exists for it, and barred any further rectangle, frame or border. Same geometry, but described as one body rather than as a count of shapes.

FIG. 4's ungrounded 38 anchor was a geometry problem, not a wording problem: the bearing face line and the exposed face line are separated only by the clearance, so any two anchors on them converge. I separated them along the sheet instead of across it, by making the column narrower than the bands and standing over the left-hand part of the area, leaving an open stretch of the exposed face line to the right for 38 while 26 stays on the bottom line of the column. This is a fragmentary enlarged view, so a column narrower than the bands is an ordinary depiction, not an added structural feature.

FIG. 5's missing terminal dot on 46 and the corner hit on 24 both came from thin, ambiguous target geometry. The pulling element is now one unbroken curved path of even thickness crossing an open expanse of tile and broken off well inside the drawing area, with a broad target anywhere on that stretch; the band gets the same visible-front-surface treatment as FIG. 1 and its target is the long stretch facing the viewer, away from either end where the band turns, which is the language the rejecting reviews were applying.

I resisted the temptation to fix any of these by changing the patent text. The connection line, the column proportions and the ring framing are all depiction conventions confined to the briefs; nothing about a duct, a port, a ledge, or a handle shape entered the description, the claims or the numeral table. The only text edits were the two sentences describing what FIG. 2 shows, and they were narrowed to the depiction rather than widened.

Trimming was necessary because the repairs added constraint sentences and every brief was already close to the length ceiling. I cut redundant view boilerplate and restated geometry rather than any of the new endpoint or topology constraints, so all five briefs now sit under the limit with the substantive instructions intact.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only, every outline one thin unbroken line. The artwork is line work alone; apart from the view legend and sheet number, the only characters are the listed reference numerals and their leader lines. The whole of the drawing stands clear of the edges of the sheet.

- 24

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work, no shading or hatching, every line solid. The preflight finding is fixed, and I applied the same treatment to the other briefs so the check does not resurface on a different sheet.

**FIG. 3 (the flagged sheet):** the blanket exclusion sentence is gone. The two-outline requirement that cured the earlier "three nested rectangles" failure is now carried positively: the sheet shows one rectangular ring and nothing else; the ring is drawn with two closed thin lines and those two alone, its outer edge and its inner edge; the slab's outer edge coincides with the ring's outer edge, that one line serving as the outline of both; and the opening is left plain so the finished sheet carries just those two closed lines. The view line likewise states what to draw, outline line work only, every outline one thin unbroken line, instead of listing line types to avoid.

**FIG. 2:** the list forbidding any gap, slot, opening, duct, port or vertical line through the slab is replaced by the positive statements that the slab is one continuous piece hatched without interruption from end to end, that its upper and lower edge lines each run whole from one end to the other, and that the slab stays whole beneath the housing whose position alone conveys the fluid communication. That preserves the constraint that cured the split-base defect.

**FIG. 1, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5:** the "No lettering, marking or border" clause became "The artwork is line work alone"; FIG. 4's "with no step, notch or cutout" and "no other horizontal line crosses it" became a plain upright rectangle whose hatching continues whole between its top and the line closing its bottom; FIG. 1's two housing bullets now describe plain uninterrupted front faces; and FIG. 5's cord is described as running throughout as one simple open curve. The remaining negatives are narrow and tied to a named object, such as no shading in an outline view, no gap where the leg end meets the band, and the depiction-convention statements that no particular handle form or attachment formation is shown.

No numeral, endpoint target, geometric relationship, or per-sheet numeral assignment changed, so the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description, and the claims all remain in sync and untouched this turn. All sixteen numerals are still covered across the five sheets, with at most seven on any sheet, and every brief is comfortably within the length limit.

input.summary: Cleared the mechanical preflight finding on the FIG. 3 brief by replacing the blanket shape-exclusion sentence with positive, renderable statements that carry the same geometry: one rectangular ring, drawn with two closed thin lines and those two alone, the slab's outer edge coinciding with the ring's outer edge, and the opening left plain so the sheet carries just those two lines. I applied the same conversion to the comparable catch-all wording in the other four briefs, notably FIG. 2's list of forbidden gaps, slots, openings, ducts, ports and vertical lines through the slab, which is now expressed as the slab being one continuous piece with unbroken edge lines that stays whole beneath the housing. No numeral, endpoint target, geometric relationship, or sheet membership changed, and no application text was edited this turn.
reasoning: The preflight objected to a brief that defines its geometry by what must not appear. That style was introduced last turn to stop the renderer inventing a third rectangle on FIG. 3 and a duct through the base on FIG. 2, so the repair had to keep the same constraints while stating them affirmatively. Every exclusion I removed has a positive counterpart that pins the same pixels: 'exactly two closed lines and those two alone' does the work of 'no third rectangle', and 'one continuous piece, hatched without interruption from end to end' does the work of the list of things forbidden to pass through the slab.

On FIG. 3 the single most load-bearing sentence was the one explaining why no separate slab outline exists. Stated negatively it read as a prohibition the model could satisfy by drawing the slab elsewhere; stated positively, the slab's outer edge coincides with the ring's outer edge and that one line serves as the outline of both, which tells the renderer what to draw rather than what to withhold.

I extended the fix beyond the flagged sheet on purpose. The same catch-all construction appeared in the view lines of FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 and in FIG. 4's 'no step, notch or cutout', so leaving them would have invited the identical finding on a different sheet next run. The negatives I kept are narrow and attached to a named object, such as no shading in an outline view and no gap where a leg end meets the band, which are ordinary drawing conventions rather than blanket shape exclusions.

FIG. 2's fluid-communication sentence needed care. Dropping the exclusion entirely risked the renderer drawing a duct that a semantic reviewer would then flag as an undescribed feature, so the positive phrasing states that the housing's position alone conveys the communication and that the slab stays whole beneath it, which both describes the intended pixels and leaves no room for a route through the base.

Nothing in draft/ required a change: the briefs express the same geometry, numerals, and relationships as before, so the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description and the claims stay exactly as filed-ready, and the five-sheet plan still covers all sixteen numerals with at most seven on a sheet.
